newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola aims for 60,000 tonnes of coffee in 5 years.
newsitem.headline: Angola aims for 60,000 tonnes of coffee in 5 years.

text.p: Angola aims to increase coffee production to as much as 60,000 tonnes in five years from 5,000 tonnes last year, a government official said on Saturday.
"Within five years it is realistic to think that we'll be producing 60,000 tonnes a year," said Josefa Sacko, an agronomist and adviser to Gilberto Lutucuta, Angola's Secretary of State for Coffee.
Sacko told Reuters production was already increasing in the country, after two decades of civil war, with between 8,000 to 10,000 tonnes of coffee to be produced this year.

She said the country also planned to rehabilitate some 50,000 hectares of coffee-growing land during the next five years at a cost of $20 million, for which Angola has applied to the International Coffee Organisation.
So far the Amsterdam-based Common Fund for Commodities has pledged $300,000 to conduct a market study for Angolan coffee, she said.

Before Angola gained independence from Portugal in 1975 the country was the second-largest African coffee producer and the world's largest supplier of robust coffee. In 1973, the country produced some 230,000 tonnes of coffee.

Sacko and other coffee industry analysts said the country would probably never again reach the level of production achieved before independence. Realistically, Sacko said, Angola could produce about 100,000 tonnes annually in about 20 years.

Benjamin Costello, a consultant with the Secretary of Coffee, agrees with that assessment. "We will never see 200,000 tonnes of production in Angola again. The Portuguese had huge farms that depended on slave labour. Angolans will never accept that again," he said.

Costello said the government would concentrate on developing small farms of a few hectares each. But to boost production significantly, he argued the government had to start paying peasants more than the 115,000 kwanzas (50 cents) per kilogram of coffee they were currently receiving.
Farmers in areas still controlled by the former rebel movement UNITA, on the other hand, fetched about one dollar a kilo.

Up to 70 percent of Angola's coffee-growing regions are still controlled by UNITA. But a recent power-sharing deal between UNITA and Angola's ruling party and plans to extend government administration to rebel-held territory are expected to increase the likelihood that those areas would soon be opened for export production.
"With the unity government now in place we will soon be able to turn our attention to increasing production in the former UNITA areas," Sacko said.
She estimated that UNITA-held areas produced at least 5,000 tonnes of coffee last year, nearly all of it was sold in Zaire.
Sacko played down the potential problems of landmines in the UNITA areas. While many supply roads were mined, plantations were not, she said.
Some estimates put the number of landmines from the country's 20-year civil war at 10 million. About 70,000 Angolans have lost limbs to the mines.

Angola's coffee exports come mainly from large farms in government-held areas, some as large as 5,000 hectares, Sacko said. She said all of the country's coffee farm owners, as well as the 10 licensed exporters, were Angolans.
April export prices for Angolan robusta coffee is about $1,15 per kilo.
Sacko also said her office wanted to focus on increasing production of Angola arabica coffee, currently selling for about three dollars a kilo on the international market.

"Arabica coffee only makes up about two percent of coffee grown here," said Sacko. "But we would like very much to expand it. There are areas in the southern part of the country that are very well suited for arabica."
